DEFINITION & OBJECTIVES
What is Green Data Science?
Definition
Green Data Science refers to developing, deploying, and managing data-driven systems while minimizing environmental impact and maximizing resource efficiency.
Core Objectives
Reduce energy consumption in data pipelines
Lower carbon emissions from computing
Improve computational efficiency
Support sustainable decision-making



WHY IT MATTERS
The Digital Sustainability Challenge
Exponential Data Growth
Global data generation is exploding — and every byte has an energy cost.
AI's Appetite for Power
AI and cloud computing demand enormous computational resources, driving up electricity consumption.
Real-World Example
Streaming platforms process billions of requests daily. Data centers consume massive electricity and water.
The result: a pressing need for sustainable computing practices across the entire data pipeline.

Sustainability in Data-Driven Systems
Sustainable Data Systems Use:
Efficient algorithms
Green cloud computing
Energy-aware ML models
Optimized storage systems
🌾 Case Study – Smart Agriculture
Data Science predicts rainfall, optimizes water usage, and improves crop yield — reducing water wastage and enabling sustainable farming.

Environmental Impact of Large-Scale Computing
Large-scale computing includes AI, Big Data, Cloud Computing, and Streaming platforms. Students usually don't realize: The cloud is someone else's computer.
Netflix
Millions of videos streamed every minute — requires servers, storage, network bandwidth, and electricity.
Google
Processes billions of searches every day across globally distributed data centers.
Amazon
Runs millions of cloud services powering businesses and consumers worldwide.

What is Carbon Footprint?
Carbon footprint is the total greenhouse gases produced due to an activity.
Formula: Carbon Footprint = Energy Consumption × Carbon Emission Factor
Every device we use draws electricity. That electricity is generated by power plants — many of which burn fossil fuels and release CO₂.
Electricity
Energy drawn by devices, starting the chain.
Power Plant
Generates electricity and determines emission intensity.
CO₂ Emissions
Emissions produced based on generation mix.
Carbon Footprint
Overall impact from devices' energy use.
Real-Life Example: Charging a laptop, smartphone, or cloud servers all contribute indirectly to carbon emissions.

Case Study – Face Recognition: Cameras, cloud storage, GPU servers, and continuous inference — carbon footprint accumulates throughout the pipeline.

Energy Consumption in Training and Inference
🏋️ Training Phase
The most resource-intensive stage. Consumes:
GPU clusters running for days or weeks
Massive cloud infrastructure
Cooling systems to prevent overheating
⚡ Inference Phase
Serves real users continuously. Consumes:
CPU and memory per request
Network resources at scale
Repeated millions of times daily
💬 Case Study – ChatGPT
Training is extremely resource-intensive. Inference serves millions of users every day — students can relate immediately.

Efficiency vs Accuracy Trade-Off
Increasing accuracy and model size also increases energy consumption, training cost, and carbon footprint.
Is the extra 1% accuracy worth 5× the energy?

Green Computing Techniques
Why These Techniques Matter
Each technique targets a different stage of the AI pipeline to 
reduce energy use, cost, and carbon emissions.
🔁 Case Study – Transfer Learning


Instead of training ResNet from scratch, use a pre-trained ResNet → less time, less energy, lower computational cost.
This single technique can reduce training energy by orders of magnitude while achieving comparable accuracy.

Case Study – Google's Green Data Centers
AI-Based Cooling
Machine learning predicts temperature and cooling requirements in real time.
Renewable Energy
Powered by solar and wind — sustainable infrastructure at global scale.
Energy-Efficient Servers
Custom hardware designed to minimize energy utilization per computation.
Reduced Emissions
Cooling energy consumption cut significantly — improving overall sustainability.

Assignment (CO1 – Analyze Level)
Title: Green Data Science for Sustainability – Case Study Analysis Report
Question:
Select any one real-world organization, application, or technology (e.g., Google Green Data Centers, Netflix, ChatGPT, Smart Agriculture, Smart Cities, Amazon Web Services, etc.) and prepare a report (3–5 pages) analyzing how Green Data Science principles are used to promote sustainability and address environmental challenges.
Your report should include:
Introduction of the selected case study. 
Environmental challenges associated with the system (energy consumption, carbon footprint, resource utilization, etc.). 
Green Data Science techniques adopted (if any). 
Analysis of how sustainability is achieved. 
Impact on Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs). 
Suggestions for making the system more energy-efficient and environmentally friendly. 
Conclusion.

Questions 
Q1:A company has two machine learning models for fraud detection. Model A provides 99% accuracy but requires 8 GPUs for training, whereas Model B provides 97% accuracy and uses only one GPU. As a Green Data Scientist, analyze which model you would recommend and justify your choice based on sustainability and energy consumption.
Q2:A farming organization uses sensors and data analytics to predict rainfall and optimize irrigation. Analyze how Green Data Science can help reduce water wastage and promote sustainable agriculture in this scenario.
